title: Area I review: Preflight Preparation
intro: These questions mix the three Tasks of Area I: pilot qualifications, weather information and cross-country planning. Many join two of them in one real IFR preflight, the way an examiner would ask.

questions.q: You plan an IFR trip at 6,000 ft: 189 NM on a true course of 270°, then 42 NM farther west to your alternate. The forecast requires an alternate. Your TAS is 135 knots and you burn 10 GPH. The FB for 6,000 ft reads 2730+05. Ignoring taxi and climb, what is the least fuel 14 CFR 91.167 lets you start with?
options: About 25.5 gallons
About 29.5 gallons
About 24.6 gallons
About 22.0 gallons
questions.why: FB winds are true, so 2730 is 270° at 30 kt, a direct headwind: groundspeed 135 - 30 = 105 kt [[28:405|AWH 27-4]]. Destination: 189 / 105 = 1.8 hr (108 min). Alternate: 42 / 105 = 0.4 hr (24 min). Then 45 minutes at normal cruise [[60:468|14 CFR 91.167(a)(1)]] [[60:469|14 CFR 91.167(a)(2)-(3)]]. 108 + 24 + 45 = 177 min = 2.95 hr x 10 GPH = 29.5 gal. 25.5 leaves out the alternate, 24.6 ignores the wind and 22.0 drops the 45 minutes.

questions.q: On a dark night you take off into low clouds and accelerate after you clean up the airplane. Suddenly you feel the nose pitching up steeply. What is happening, and what do you do?
options: The elevator illusion; lower the nose until the feeling stops
The leans; level the wings by feel, then check the instruments
A real pitch-up from wind shear; push forward hard right away
The somatogravic illusion; hold the attitude the instruments show
questions.why: Rapid acceleration stimulates the inner ear the same way as tilting the head back. This somatogravic illusion feels like a nose-up attitude, and the disoriented pilot may push into a dive [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]. Trust the instruments and disregard your sensations [[23:76|IFH 3-9]]. The elevator illusion comes from an updraft, not from speeding up [[23:73|IFH 3-6]].

questions.q: The TAF for your departure airport at takeoff time reads 18008KT P6SM OVC020 WS015/25045KT. What does the WS group tell you?
options: Wind shear from the surface to 1,500 ft, with 250° at 45 kt at the top
A 45-knot change in wind speed somewhere below 1,500 ft
Wind shear near 15,000 ft, with the wind from 250° at 45 kt
Surface gusts to 45 kt from 250° starting at 1500Z
questions.why: WS is followed by the top of the wind shear layer (015 = 1,500 ft), and low-level wind shear is forecast from the surface up to it. The wind group after the slash is the wind at the top of the layer, not the amount of shear [[28:416|AWH 27-15]]. So the wind goes from 180° at 8 kt at the surface to 250° at 45 kt at 1,500 ft, right in your initial climb.

questions.q: Use the figure. You fly the V465 segment shown on the low chart with an IFR-approved WAAS GPS and pick up ice at 15,000 ft. The freezing level is reported at 14,000 ft. What is the lowest altitude you may request on this segment to get into warmer air?
options: 15,000 ft, the MEA for the segment
14,000 ft, just at the freezing level
13,300 ft, the GNSS MEA for the segment
13,300 ft, but only within 22 NM of the VOR
questions.why: Blue altitudes with a G suffix are GNSS MEAs, added to Victor airways for aircraft flying them with GPS [[2:69|Chart Users' Guide p 69]]. A GNSS MEA assures GPS reception and obstacle clearance on the segment [[34:353|AIM P/C Glossary]]. The *13300 is a MOCA, and the 22 NM limit applies only when you navigate by VOR [[60:480|14 CFR 91.177(a)(1)]]. With GPS, 13,300 ft is good for the whole segment and puts you below the freezing level.

questions.q: You fell out of instrument currency two months ago, so you don't need an IPC yet. Today the clouds are low and you want to fly your approaches, holding and tracking in actual conditions. How can you do that legally?
options: You can't; the tasks must be flown under a view-limiting device
Fly IFR with a current, qualified pilot such as a CFII acting as PIC
File IFR yourself; flights to regain currency are exempt from 61.57
You can't; only an IPC can make you current again at this point
questions.why: Until you are current you may not act as PIC under IFR or in weather below VFR minimums [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)]], so a current, qualified pilot must be PIC. The tasks may be flown in actual weather conditions [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)(1)]], and you log instrument time while you fly solely by instruments [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(1)]]. An IPC is needed only after more than six calendar months out of currency [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(1)]].

questions.q: It rained all afternoon at your departure airport. Tonight the sky is clearing, the wind is calm and the temperature-dewpoint spread is 2 °C. You plan to leave IFR at 0600, before sunrise. What should you plan for?
options: Good weather, since the rain washed the moisture out of the air
Advection fog, which forms only when a strong wind blows in
Radiation fog, which often doesn't clear until after sunrise
Thunderstorms, since the wet ground heats quickly at dawn
questions.why: Clear skies, light wind and moist air near the ground favor radiation fog, and it is not uncommon the morning after rain soaks the ground and the sky clears [[28:223|AWH 18-3]]. It is generally a nighttime event that often does not dissipate until after sunrise [[28:222|AWH 18-2]]. Expect low visibility at 0600 and plan a later departure or a way out if it forms.

questions.q: Your filed airway crosses a MOA that will be active when you get there. What does the AIM say ATC will do with your IFR flight?
options: Clear you through if it can keep IFR separation, or else reroute you
Clear you through, since IFR traffic has priority over the military
Leave it to you to call the controlling agency for permission
Cancel your IFR clearance so you can go around the MOA under VFR
questions.why: When a MOA is in use, nonparticipating IFR traffic may be cleared through it if ATC can provide IFR separation. Otherwise ATC will reroute or restrict the IFR traffic [[33:191|AIM 3-4-5a]]. Check MOA times in your briefing so a reroute doesn't surprise your fuel plan.

questions.q: Your club's single-engine airplane has a single throwover control wheel instead of dual yokes. A private pilot friend offers to be your safety pilot while you practice approaches under a view-limiting device. Is that allowed?
options: No, simulated instrument flight always needs full dual controls
Yes, but only if your friend also holds an instrument rating
No, a throwover wheel may be used only for flight instruction
Yes, if the safety pilot decides the flight can be done safely
questions.why: Simulated instrument flight may be done in a single-engine airplane with a functioning throwover wheel when the safety pilot has determined the flight can be conducted safely and the person flying has at least a private pilot certificate [[60:447|14 CFR 91.109(c)(3)]]. The safety pilot needs at least a private pilot certificate with the right category and class, not an instrument rating [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)]].

questions.q: The METAR at your departure airport reports FZRA with a temperature of -2 °C. What does that tell you about the air above you?
options: The whole column of air from the ground up is below freezing
A deep above-freezing layer lies over a shallow freezing layer
A shallow warm layer lies over a deep freezing layer at the ground
Temperature falls steadily with height, as in a standard atmosphere
questions.why: Freezing rain needs a deep layer of above-freezing air aloft over a shallow below-freezing layer at the surface: a temperature inversion, often along a warm front [[28:168|AWH 14-4]]. A shallow warm layer over a deep cold layer makes ice pellets instead [[28:168|AWH 14-4]]. The drops freeze on contact with the airplane [[28:169|AWH 14-5]].

questions.q: You plan a direct leg off the airways, with no published minimum altitude, over an area designated as mountainous. The highest obstacle within 4 NM of your course is a tower at 6,340 ft MSL. A 7,100 ft peak sits 6 NM off course. What is the lowest IFR altitude 14 CFR 91.177 allows?
options: 7,340 ft MSL
9,100 ft MSL
8,340 ft MSL
8,100 ft MSL
questions.why: With no published minimum altitude, over a designated mountainous area you must stay 2,000 ft above the highest obstacle within 4 NM of the course [[60:480|14 CFR 91.177(a)(2)(i)]]. The peak is 6 NM away, so it doesn't count: 6,340 + 2,000 = 8,340 ft MSL. 7,340 uses the 1,000 ft rule for areas that are not mountainous [[60:480|14 CFR 91.177(a)(2)(ii)]].

questions.q: On a 1.8-hour IFR flight you hand-fly 0.6 hour in the clouds, then 0.4 hour under a view-limiting device with a safety pilot, and the last 0.8 hour in clear air looking outside. How much instrument time may you log?
options: 1.0 hour
0.6 hour
0.4 hour
1.8 hours
questions.why: You may log instrument time only while you fly solely by reference to instruments, in actual or simulated conditions [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(1)]]. That is 0.6 actual + 0.4 simulated = 1.0 hour. Being on an IFR flight plan doesn't make the 0.8 hour in clear air instrument time.

questions.q: During your preflight briefing you see a severe thunderstorm with an intense radar echo sitting 12 miles off your planned airway, with its anvil spreading toward the route. What does the AIM advise?
options: Keep the route, since 12 miles is enough room for one storm
Keep the route, but fly under the anvil to stay out of the cloud
Keep the route and use FIS-B radar in flight to slip past it
Plan a route that stays at least 20 miles away from the storm
questions.why: Avoid by at least 20 miles any thunderstorm identified as severe or giving an intense radar echo, especially under the anvil of a large cumulonimbus [[34:120|AIM 7-1-27a14]]. Don't fly under the anvil, and don't use data-linked NEXRAD as the only way through a thunderstorm area [[34:120|AIM 7-1-27a]].

questions.q: Use the figure. Your airplane is approach Category A. You want to list Cortez Muni as your alternate, planning on the VOR Rwy 21 approach. What forecast must Cortez have at your ETA?
options: Ceiling 900 ft and visibility 3 SM
Ceiling 800 ft and visibility 2 SM
Ceiling 600 ft and visibility 2 SM
Ceiling 1,300 ft and visibility 2 SM
questions.why: Note 1 for the VOR Rwy 21 changes the alternate minimums only for Category D, to 900-3 [[29:29|IPH 1-13]]. A Category A airplane uses the standard minimums for a nonprecision approach: ceiling 800 ft and visibility 2 SM [[60:470|14 CFR 91.169(c)(1)(i)(B)]]. 600-2 is for precision approaches, and 1300-2 is note 2, for the RNAV (GPS) Z.

questions.q: You plan a flight from a mountain airport at 4,200 ft elevation. The FB for that location has columns for 3,000, 6,000 and 9,000 ft. What will you find in the 6,000 ft column?
options: A wind forecast but no temperature
Both a wind and a temperature forecast
A temperature forecast but no wind
Nothing, since it is too close to the field
questions.why: Wind forecasts are not issued for altitudes within 1,500 ft of a location's elevation, and temperature forecasts are not issued within 2,500 ft [[28:405|AWH 27-4]]. 6,000 ft is 1,800 ft above the field: more than 1,500 ft, so a wind is given; less than 2,500 ft, so no temperature.

questions.q: You are hand-flying a long, steady turn in the clouds when your tablet slides to the floor. You bend down and turn your head to grab it, and suddenly feel the airplane turning on a different axis. What is this, and how could you have avoided it?
options: The leans; roll level slowly before you reach for anything
Autokinesis; stop staring at one light before looking down
The coriolis illusion; keep head movement to a minimum
The inversion illusion; level off before you reach for it
questions.why: After a long turn the inner-ear fluid moves with the canal. A head movement in another plane sets it moving again and creates the coriolis illusion of turning on a different axis. Use a scan with minimal head movement, and retrieve dropped items with as little head movement as you can [[23:73|IFH 3-6]].

questions.q: To top an icing layer you plan to cruise for an hour at 15,500 ft MSL in an unpressurized airplane with two passengers. What does 14 CFR 91.211 require?
options: You use oxygen after the first 30 minutes; passengers need none
Everyone aboard must use oxygen the whole time at that altitude
You use oxygen the whole time; passengers only above 16,000 ft
You use oxygen the whole time, and each passenger is provided it
questions.why: Above 14,000 ft cabin altitude the required crew must use oxygen for the entire time at those altitudes, and above 15,000 ft each occupant must be provided with oxygen [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)(2)-(3)]]. The rule requires the passengers to be provided with oxygen, not to use it. The 30-minute allowance applies only above 12,500 up to 14,000 ft [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)(1)]].

questions.q: Use the figure. A storm 10 miles from your destination has just started dropping rain to the ground. You are 15 minutes out. What does that stage of the storm mean for your arrival?
options: It is mature, and its gust front can spread well ahead of it
It is in the towering cumulus stage, with updrafts but no hazards
It is dissipating, so its hazards are already dying out
It is mature, but its strong winds stay under the rain shaft
questions.why: A cell becomes mature when precipitation reaches the surface. Its downdraft spreads out along the surface well in advance of the storm as a cool, gusty gust front, and hazards peak toward the end of the mature stage [[28:258|AWH 22-3]]. Don't land or take off in the face of an approaching thunderstorm [[34:119|AIM 7-1-27a1]].

questions.q: You usually fly a fast high-performance single. Today you rent a slower trainer for the same IFR trip, into a forecast headwind. What does AC 90-109A tell you to expect?
options: The same time and fuel plan, since the wind is the same
A bigger hit from the headwind and stronger weather effects
Easier handling and fewer surprises than the faster airplane
Better avionics, since trainers are built for IFR training
questions.why: Moving to a lower-performance airplane, weather effects are more pronounced, the headwind takes a bigger percentage of your speed, turbulence may feel worse and the avionics may be less capable [[57:52|AC 90-109A App 10, 2]]. So rework your time, fuel and alternatives for this airplane before the flight [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(a)]].

questions.q: Your airplane has two independent VOR receivers, and the last VOR check was 40 days ago. The airport has no VOT or checkpoint, so you tune both receivers to the same VOR. They show 093° and 098°. May you use the VORs under IFR?
options: Yes, because the dual-check limit is 6°
Yes, because a check is needed only every 60 days
No, because the 5° difference is more than 4°
No, because a dual check may be done only in flight
questions.why: To use VOR under IFR, the equipment must have been checked within the preceding 30 days, so you need a check today [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(a)(2)]]. In a dual check both receivers are tuned to the same VOR, and the bearings may differ by at most 4° [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(c)]]. 098 - 093 = 5°, so it fails. The 6° limit is for airborne checkpoints [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)(3)]].

questions.q: Your destination TAF reads FM202000 19010KT P6SM SCT050 PROB30 2022/2024 2SM TSRA OVC020CB. Your ETA is 2300Z. How should you read the PROB30 group?
options: A 30 percent chance of a 2,000 ft ceiling any time after 2000Z
A forecast of thunderstorms starting on the 22nd of the month
Temporary thunderstorms with a greater than 50 percent chance
A low, 30 percent chance of thunderstorms from 2200Z to 2400Z
questions.why: PROB30 forecasts a low-probability (30 percent) thunderstorm or precipitation event with its wind, visibility and sky. The first two digits are the day, the next two the start hour; after the slash come the end day and hour [[28:418|AWH 27-17]]. So 2022/2024 is the 20th, 2200Z to 2400Z, which covers your ETA. A greater than 50 percent chance is a TEMPO group [[28:417|AWH 27-16]].

questions.q: After six months of steady IFR flying, you feel ready to lower your day IFR personal minimums. What does the RMH advise?
options: Change one value at a time, at a calm time with no trip pending
Lower ceiling and visibility together so they stay matched
Lower them on the morning of a trip you really want to make
Drop them straight down to the published approach minimums
questions.why: Don't adjust personal minimums to complete a specific flight; make changes when time and objectivity allow an honest self-analysis. Adjust one variable at a time: if you lower visibility, leave the ceiling and other values alone [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

questions.q: Eastbound on an airway at 5,000 ft, you reach a fix where the MEA rises to 9,000 ft. An MCA of 7,500 ft eastbound is charted at the fix because of terrain just beyond it. What does 14 CFR 91.177 require?
options: Start the climb to 9,000 ft right after you pass the fix
Cross the fix at or above 7,500 ft, then keep climbing to 9,000 ft
Reach 9,000 ft before the fix, then cross it at the new MEA
Cross the fix at 5,000 ft and reach 7,500 ft within 22 NM
questions.why: Normally you start climbing to a higher MEA right after passing the fix, but when ground obstructions intervene you must cross that fix at or above the MCA [[60:480|14 CFR 91.177(b)]]. An MCA is the lowest altitude at which you must cross the fix toward a higher MEA [[2:69|Chart Users' Guide p 69]]. So be at 7,500 ft or higher at the fix, then continue to 9,000 ft.

questions.q: You fly four approaches under a view-limiting device with a friend as safety pilot, to count toward your six-month instrument experience. What must your logbook show for them?
options: Only the total instrument time and the date of the flight
Your friend's signature and pilot certificate number
The location and type of each approach and the safety pilot's name
An instructor's endorsement for each of the approaches flown
questions.why: To log instrument time for 61.57(c) currency, record the location and type of each instrument approach and the name of the safety pilot, if one is required [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(3)]]. A safety pilot is required for simulated instrument flight [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)]].

questions.q: Lens-shaped clouds sit in bands parallel to a mountain ridge, downwind of it. Your approach to an airport on that side of the ridge goes beneath them. What should you expect?
options: Smooth air, since lenticular clouds form only in stable air
Icing only, since the clouds are made of supercooled drops
Turbulence only well above the clouds, never below them
Gusty, variable winds and moderate-to-severe turbulence below
questions.why: Bands of standing lenticular clouds downwind of a ridge mark trapped lee waves, a concern for takeoff and landing [[28:197|AWH 16-8]]. Below lenticular clouds the wind can be variable and gusty, and PIREPs often report moderate-to-severe turbulence beneath the clouds [[28:198|AWH 16-9]].
